title: Data Cleaning & Wrangling
blurb: Tests whether you can diagnose and treat missing values, outliers, duplicates, wrong types, encoding errors and messy categories, and predict what the pandas cleaning code does.

ideas.title: Duplicates and the index after removal
Validation, cleaning order and leakage-safe pipelines

questions.prompt: Missingness that depends on **observed** variables, but not on the missing value itself, is called what?
options: Structural missingness
MNAR (Missing Not At Random)
MCAR (Missing Completely At Random)
MAR (Missing At Random)
questions.explanation: MAR means the chance of a gap depends on variables you can see, not on the hidden value. It can be imputed safely if the imputer uses those predictive variables. MCAR depends on nothing at all. MNAR depends on the missing value itself. The names are confusing because MAR is not "random" in everyday language.

questions.prompt: Why is the IQR method more robust to one extreme value than the z-score method?
options: The IQR method uses a larger multiplier than the z-score method, so it flags fewer points
$Q_1$ and $Q_3$ are rank statistics, so an extreme value barely moves them, while it inflates $\sigma$
The IQR method assumes the data are normal, which makes its bounds more precise
The z-score method ignores the largest value when it computes the mean
questions.explanation: Quartiles depend on sorted position, not magnitude. Move the maximum from 100 to 100,000 and $Q_1$, $Q_3$ stay put. A z-score uses $\mu$ and $\sigma$, which the outlier itself pulls up, so it can mask itself. It is the z-score method, not IQR, that assumes approximate normality.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter call duplicate rows "quietly catastrophic" for machine learning?
options: sklearn raises an error when two rows are identical, which stops the pipeline
They double the memory the DataFrame needs, which slows down every later cleaning step
Copies land in both train and test sets, so the test score rewards memorisation
They always pull the mean of every numeric column towards zero, biasing the fit
questions.explanation: Duplicates corrupt evaluation, not only training. A test row that also sits in the training set has been seen, so accuracy is inflated. The gap only shows up in production. sklearn raises no error for duplicate rows, which is why the problem is quiet.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a **schema violation** rather than a type problem?
options: A `hire_date` column left as text because it was never parsed
A `quantity` column that holds `'12'` as a string instead of the number 12
A `price` column loaded as text, so `'10' > '9'` is `False`
An `age` column of integers that contains `-5`
questions.explanation: `-5` parses as a perfectly good integer. It has the right type but breaks the rule of what an age can mean. The other three are type problems. The value has not been converted to the type it should be. Type coercion asks "can this be parsed?". A schema rule asks "is this value allowed?".

questions.prompt: A city column shows `SÃ£o Paulo` where `São Paulo` was expected. The file was UTF-8 but was read as Latin-1. Which expression repairs one mangled string `s`?
options: `s.lower().strip()`
`s.encode('ascii', errors='ignore').decode('ascii')`
`s.encode('latin1').decode('utf-8')`
`s.encode('utf-8').decode('latin1')`
questions.explanation: Run the mistake backwards. Encoding as Latin-1 recovers the original bytes. Decoding those bytes as UTF-8 gives the real text. The reverse order is the operation that caused the damage. Dropping non-ASCII characters gives `So Paulo`, which is a new error.

questions.prompt: According to the chapter, which step is never optional after a cleaning operation?
options: Winsorise every numeric column at the 1st and 99th percentile
Validate rules and compare before/after distributions of touched columns
Impute every missing value, including those in the target column
Drop every row that still has a missing value in any column
questions.explanation: Validation is the one step the chapter calls never optional. A cleaning step can silently collapse meaningful variation, and only a before/after comparison shows it. Imputing the target is forbidden, not required. It is label fabrication.

questions.prompt: In a clinic dataset, systolic blood pressure is missing more often for patients whose pressure is very high, because they are sent straight to emergency care before the reading is logged. What is the mechanism, and what happens with mean imputation?
options: MAR. Mean imputation is safe because missingness depends on another variable
MNAR. Mean imputation will overestimate average blood pressure
MCAR. Mean imputation adds no bias because the gaps are random
MNAR. Mean imputation will underestimate average blood pressure
questions.explanation: Missingness depends on the missing value itself (high readings go missing), so it is MNAR. The observed readings are skewed low, so filling gaps with their mean pulls the estimate down. MAR would need the gaps to depend on an observed variable, not on the pressure.

questions.prompt:
What is the mean of `f`? Give a decimal to 2 d.p.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([2, 4, np.nan, 10, np.nan, 50])
f = s.fillna(s.median())
f.mean()
```
questions.explanation: `median()` skips NaN. The observed values are 2, 4, 10, 50, so the median is $(4+10)/2 = 7$. Both gaps get 7. The filled series is `[2, 4, 7, 10, 7, 50]`, with sum 80 and mean $80/6 = 13.33$. The original observed mean was $66/4 = 16.5$. Median filling pulled it down towards the bulk of the data.

questions.prompt: Response times (ms) are `[12, 15, 17, 18, 20, 21, 22, 25, 60]`. Using pandas' default `quantile` (linear interpolation) and $k = 1.5$, what is the **upper** IQR fence? Give a decimal to 1 d.p.
questions.explanation: With 9 sorted values, $Q_1$ sits at position $0.25 \times 8 = 2$ (zero-based), which is 17. $Q_3$ sits at position 6, which is 22. $\text{IQR} = 22 - 17 = 5$. Upper fence $= 22 + 1.5 \times 5 = 29.5$. Only 60 lies above it. The lower fence is $17 - 7.5 = 9.5$.

questions.prompt:
What does this print?

```python
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3],
                   'ts': [1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
                   'v':  ['a', 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'c']})
print(df.duplicated().sum(),
      len(df.drop_duplicates(subset=['id'], keep='last')))
```
questions.explanation: `duplicated()` with no subset needs every column to match an earlier row. Only row 1 copies row 0. Row 5 `(3, 5, 'c')` shares `id` and `v` with row 3 but its `ts` differs, so it is not an exact duplicate. With `subset=['id']`, one row per id survives. Ids 1, 2 and 3 give 3 rows.

questions.prompt:
What does this print?

```python
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(['12', '7', 'n/a', '3.5', '', '1,000'])
x = pd.to_numeric(s, errors='coerce')
print(x.isna().sum(), x.sum())
```
questions.explanation: `errors='coerce'` turns anything that does not parse into NaN. `'n/a'`, the empty string and `'1,000'` (the comma is not a valid number character) all fail, so there are 3 NaN values. The rest sum to $12 + 7 + 3.5 = 22.5$. Silently losing the `1,000` row is why you check `isna()` straight after coercing.

questions.prompt:
A column of order counts was read as text. What does this return?

```python
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(['9', '10', '100', '25'])
s.max()
```
questions.explanation: Strings compare character by character. `'9'` beats `'1…'` and `'2…'` at the first character, so it is the lexical maximum. No error is raised. The result is still a string. Converting with `pd.to_numeric` first would give 100.

questions.prompt:
What does this print?

```python
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([' Male', 'F', 'female ', 'MALE', 'Mal', 'woman', 'm'])
mapping = {'male': 'male', 'm': 'male', 'man': 'male',
           'female': 'female', 'f': 'female', 'woman': 'female'}
out = s.str.strip().str.lower().map(mapping)
print(out.value_counts().to_dict(), out.isna().sum())
```
options: `{'male': 2, 'female': 3} 2`
`{'male': 4, 'female': 3} 0`
`{'male': 3, 'female': 2} 2`
`{'male': 3, 'female': 3} 1`
questions.explanation: After strip and lowercase the values are `male, f, female, male, mal, woman, m`. `male` appears twice plus `m`, giving 3 male. `f`, `female` and `woman` give 3 female. `mal` is not in the mapping, so `.map()` turns it into NaN. That silent NaN is why you must check what is left unmapped.

questions.prompt:
The rules from Listing 7.6 run on this DataFrame. Select ALL rules that print `FAILED`.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'age':    [25, 40, 31, 25],
                   'salary': [50000, np.nan, 48000, 50000]})
```
options: No duplicate rows
All salaries positive
No missing values
All ages >= 16
questions.explanation: The NaN salary fails the missing-values rule. Rows 0 and 3 are identical, so the duplicate rule fails. Every age is at least 16. The salary rule also fails, even though no salary is zero or negative. `NaN > 0` is `False`, so `.all()` returns `False`. A NaN can trip every comparison rule on its column.

questions.prompt: `s = pd.Series([2., 4., 6., 8., np.nan, np.nan])`. `s.var()` is 6.67. What is the sample variance after `s.fillna(s.mean())`? Give a decimal to 2 d.p.
questions.explanation: The observed mean is 5, so both gaps become 5. The mean stays 5. The squared deviations are $9, 1, 1, 9, 0, 0$, sum 20. Dividing by $n - 1 = 5$ gives a variance of $20/5 = 4.00$. The spread drops from 6.67 to 4.00 because two points were placed exactly at the centre. Mean imputation keeps the mean but shrinks the variance, which makes later confidence intervals too narrow.

questions.prompt: Values are `[10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 100]`. Using the population standard deviation (NumPy's default `ddof=0`), what is the z-score of 100? Give a decimal to 2 d.p.
questions.explanation: $\mu = 160/6 = 26.67$. The squared deviations sum to about 6463.3, so $\sigma = \sqrt{6463.3/6} \approx 32.82$. Then $z = (100 - 26.67)/32.82 \approx 2.23$. That is below 3, so the z-score rule does not flag an obvious error. The outlier inflated $\sigma$ and masked itself. The IQR rule catches it. $Q_1 = 11.25$ and $Q_3 = 13.75$, so the upper fence is $17.5$.

questions.prompt:
What does this print?

```python
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'v': [10, 10, 20, 30, 30, 40]})
df = df.drop_duplicates()
print(df.loc[3, 'v'], df.iloc[3]['v'])
```
options: A `KeyError` is raised
questions.explanation: `drop_duplicates()` keeps the original labels, so the index becomes `[0, 2, 3, 5]` with values `[10, 20, 30, 40]`. `.loc[3]` finds label 3, which is 30. `.iloc[3]` is the fourth row by position, which is 40. This is the gap the chapter warns about. Add `.reset_index(drop=True)` after dropping.

questions.prompt:
What does this print?

```python
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(['34', '-5', 'abc', '41', '130'])
age = pd.to_numeric(s, errors='coerce')
valid = age.between(16, 90)
print(age.isna().sum(), (~valid).sum())
```
questions.explanation: Coercion catches only the type problem. `'abc'` becomes NaN, so 1 missing value. `-5` and `130` parse fine. They are schema violations that only the range rule catches. `between` returns `False` for NaN, so `~valid` counts `-5`, NaN and `130`, which is 3. The count mixes one type failure with two schema failures, so report them separately.

questions.prompt:
How many unique values remain? Give an integer.

```python
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(['São Paulo', 'sao paulo', 'SÃ£o Paulo',
               ' São Paulo', 'Zürich', 'ZÃ¼rich'])
s.str.strip().str.lower().nunique()
```
questions.explanation: Strip and lowercase merge only `'São Paulo'` and `' São Paulo'`. The five survivors are `são paulo`, `sao paulo`, `sã£o paulo`, `zürich` and `zã¼rich`. Lowercasing fixes neither mojibake nor a missing accent. The encoding repair and an explicit mapping (`'sao paulo'` to `'são paulo'`) are still needed to reach 2 cities.

questions.prompt: Salaries (in £k) are `s = pd.Series([40, 50, 60, 70, 980, np.nan])`, where 980 is an entry error. The domain cap is 100. A pipeline runs `s.fillna(s.mean()).clip(upper=100)`. What value does the originally missing row end up with? Give a decimal to 1 d.p.
questions.explanation: Imputation runs first, so the fill value is the mean including the error, $1200/5 = 240$. The clip then caps both 980 and the imputed 240 at 100. The missing employee is recorded at the cap. In the Worked Example's order (outliers, then missingness), the cap gives `[40, 50, 60, 70, 100]` and the fill value is $320/5 = 64.0$. Order matters.

questions.prompt: True incomes (£k) for six people are `[30, 40, 50, 60, 200, 250]`. The two highest earners decline to answer. You fill their gaps with the mean of the observed incomes. By how much does the mean of the imputed column underestimate the true mean? Give a decimal to 1 d.p. (in £k).
questions.explanation: True mean $= 630/6 = 105$. The observed mean is $180/4 = 45$, and both gaps become 45. The imputed column is `[30, 40, 50, 60, 45, 45]`, whose mean is still 45. The gap is $105 - 45 = 60$. This is MNAR. The values that went missing are the large ones, so any imputation fitted only on observed incomes cannot recover them. Collecting more rows does not help. The missingness process must be modelled.

questions.prompt: Using the population standard deviation (`ddof=0`), the largest possible $|z|$ in a sample of size $n$ occurs when $n-1$ values are equal and one differs. What is the **smallest** $n$ for which any value can have $|z| > 3$? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: Put $n-1$ zeros and one value $x$. The mean is $x/n$ and the deviation of $x$ is $x(n-1)/n$. The variance is $x^2(n-1)/n^2$, so $\sigma = x\sqrt{n-1}/n$. That gives $z_{\max} = \sqrt{n-1}$. We need $\sqrt{n-1} > 3$, so $n - 1 > 9$ and $n \ge 11$. At $n = 10$ the maximum is exactly 3, which does not pass $|z| > 3$. On small samples the z-score rule cannot flag anything, however wrong the value is. Use IQR or a domain cap there.

questions.prompt:
This follows Listing 7.3. What does `unmapped` contain?

```python
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'col': ['Male', 'f', 'Mal', 'woman']})
mapping = {'male': 'male', 'm': 'male', 'man': 'male',
           'female': 'female', 'f': 'female', 'woman': 'female'}
df['col'] = df['col'].str.strip().str.lower()
df['col'] = df['col'].map(mapping)
unmapped = df[df['col'].isnull()]['col'].value_counts()
```
options: A Series with one entry, `'Mal'` with a count of 1
A Series with one entry, `NaN` with a count of 1
An empty Series, since the selected rows are all NaN
A Series with one entry, `'mal'` with a count of 1
questions.explanation: The mapping overwrote `df['col']`, so the original spelling is gone. The filter selects the rows where `col` is NaN, then counts the values in that same column. They are all NaN, and `value_counts()` excludes NaN by default, so the result is empty. The check always reports nothing to fix. Keep the pre-map column, e.g. `raw = df['col']` before mapping, then `raw[df['col'].isnull()].value_counts()` shows `'mal'`.

questions.prompt:
A column holds mostly correct city names plus a few mojibake entries. What happens when you run this repair over the **whole** column?

```python
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(['São Paulo', 'SÃ£o Paulo', 'Paris'])
s.apply(lambda t: t.encode('latin1').decode('utf-8'))
```
options: It leaves all three unchanged, because Latin-1 and UTF-8 agree on these characters
It repairs `'SÃ£o Paulo'` and leaves the other two unchanged
It turns the correct `'São Paulo'` into new mojibake and repairs the mangled one
It raises `UnicodeDecodeError` on the correct `'São Paulo'`
questions.explanation: The correct `'ã'` encodes to the single Latin-1 byte `0xE3`. In UTF-8 that byte starts a three-byte sequence, but the next byte is `'o'`, so decoding fails with `UnicodeDecodeError`. `'Paris'` would survive the round trip and the mangled entry would be repaired, but `apply` stops at the first row with the error, so neither is reached. Apply the fix only to rows that show the pattern (for example those containing `'Ã'`), or re-read the file with the right `encoding=`.

bookExercises.prompt: Classify each of the following as MCAR, MAR, or MNAR, and justify your answer in one sentence: (a) a temperature sensor that randomly drops 2% of readings due to a hardware fault; (b) a salary survey where respondents earning over \$500k are half as likely to answer the income question as everyone else; (c) a customer age field where missingness is higher among users who signed up via a mobile app that didn't require an age field, regardless of their actual age.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: (a) MCAR: a hardware fault dropping readings at random has no relationship to the reading's value or any other variable. (b) MNAR: the probability of a missing income value depends directly on the (unobserved) income itself, higher earners are more likely to decline. (c) MAR: missingness correlates with an observed variable (signup channel), not with the true age value itself. Conditional on signup channel, the missing ages aren't systematically different from the reported ones.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 7.8's logic, explain why `ages[0] = 312` is assigned after the missing-value assignment `ages[missing_age_idx] = np.nan`, and what would change about row 0 if the two lines were swapped.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The typo assignment `ages[0] = 312` is applied after the missing-value assignment so that it deterministically overwrites row 0 regardless of whether index 0 happened to be selected by `np.random.choice(n, 40, replace=False)`. If the two lines were swapped, row 0 would first be set to 312, and then, only if index 0 were among the 40 randomly chosen missing indices, get overwritten back to NaN, making the presence of the planted outlier depend on random chance rather than being guaranteed. The chapter's ordering guarantees the outlier exists every time the notebook runs with a fixed seed.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 7.9 as a reference, compute what the age imputation value would need to be if, instead of median imputation, mean imputation were used on the post-capping age column. Describe the one-line change and state whether you'd expect the result to be higher or lower than 42, and why.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The one-line change is `df['age'] = df['age'].fillna(df['age'].mean())` in place of `.median()`. Before capping, the raw `describe()` output shows a mean of 43.45 against a median of 42, the 312 outlier pulling the mean up well above the rank-based median. Capping that single value down to 90 drags the mean back down to about 42.34, very close to the median of 42. So mean imputation would land at roughly 42.3, a third of a point above the reported median-imputed value of 42, with the small remaining gap explained by the mild right skew still left in age even after the domain cap.

bookExercises.prompt: The chapter reports that IQR-based detection flags only 1 outlier in the raw age column despite there being an obvious typo (312) and a long right tail from natural variation. Using Listing 7.4's `iqr_bounds` function, explain why a single extreme value like 312 can fail to inflate the outlier count the way you might expect, given how $Q_1$ and $Q_3$ are computed.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: $Q_1$ and $Q_3$ are the 25th and 75th percentile of the whole column, and with only one value at 312 sitting far above the bulk of the data (ages naturally spread across 22 to 64), that single point has almost no leverage on the rank-based $Q_1$/$Q_3$ statistics. 312 is one point out of hundreds, so the 25th/75th percentile boundaries barely move to accommodate it, and the resulting IQR fence lands well below 312, meaning IQR does in fact catch it (that's the reported "1 outlier"). The subtler risk is the opposite one: IQR is a whole-column, single-pass method, so a handful of outliers or a long natural tail can each be caught or missed depending on how many other values sit between the bulk of the distribution and the fence, which is why the chapter still applies a domain-knowledge cap ([16, 90]) on top of IQR rather than trusting IQR's fence alone.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague proposes skipping validation (Procedure 7.6) on the grounds that "the pipeline already ran without errors, so the data must be fine." Using this chapter's Trade-offs section, write the two or three sentences you'd say to push back, with a concrete example of a silent failure that would pass unnoticed without an explicit validation step.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A pipeline running without errors only confirms that every operation was syntactically and type-valid. It says nothing about whether the result is semantically correct. A concrete silent failure: an incorrectly specified `gender_map` that's missing the `'MALE'` (all-caps) variant wouldn't raise any error. `.map()` would convert every `'MALE'` entry to NaN, silently turning a known category into missing data, and the pipeline would report success right up until someone later asks why 50 rows have a missing gender that used to have a value.

bookExercises.prompt: Design a validation rule set (in the style of Listing 7.6) for a dataset of e-commerce orders with columns `order_total`, `discount_pct`, `ship_date`, `delivery_date`, and `customer_id`. Propose at least four rules, including at least one that checks a relationship between two columns rather than a single column in isolation.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Sample rules: (1) `(d['order_total'] > 0).all()`, no order should have a non-positive total. (2) `(d['discount_pct'] >= 0).all()` and `(d['discount_pct'] <= 100).all()`, a discount percentage must be a valid percentage. (3) `d['customer_id'].notnull().all()`, every order must be attributable to a customer. (4) A cross-column rule: `(d['delivery_date'] >= d['ship_date']).all()`, a package cannot be delivered before it ships, which single-column rules can never catch since both dates can individually look valid. A fifth candidate worth adding: `(d['ship_date'] - d['order_date']).dt.days.between(0, 30).all()` as a sanity bound on fulfilment time, catching data-entry errors that swap order and ship dates.

bookExercises.prompt: MNAR missingness is described in this chapter as requiring you to "model the missingness mechanism, not just the missing value." Research one concrete technique for this (e.g. Heckman correction, pattern-mixture models, or multiple imputation with a missingness indicator) and summarise, in your own words, what data beyond the column itself it requires.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only, no single answer. Multiple imputation with a missingness indicator is the most tractable technique to start with: alongside the imputed value, an explicit binary column recording whether the value was originally missing is added as a feature, which lets a downstream model learn that "this value was estimated" is itself informative (relevant when missingness correlates with the outcome, as in MNAR). A Heckman correction goes further, formally modelling a "selection equation" for whether a value is observed at all, jointly with the equation of interest. It requires an instrument variable that affects observability but not the outcome directly, which is often the hardest part to find in practice. Worth considering: unlike MCAR/MAR imputation, none of these techniques make the MNAR problem disappear. They make its assumptions explicit and testable rather than silently violated.
